appraisal_events.evidence: 'Une fois captif chez moi... Albertine avait perdu toutes ses couleurs, avec toutes les chances qu'avaient les autres de l'avoir à eux. Elle avait peu à peu perdu sa beauté.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator states plainly that captivity has drained Albertine of the allure she had when free and desired by others at Balbec, reducing her in his eyes to a 'grise prisonnière.'

appraisal_events.evidence: Remembering Balbec: 'elle éclatait de rire en me regardant d'une façon insolente'... 'm'avait... infligé ce définitif affront' before a woman he suspected her of an affair with.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator recalls Albertine mockingly laughing at him in front of a woman he suspected her of an affair with, an insolent snub he still feels as a lasting affront; the same memory paradoxically restores her beauty and desirability in his eyes.

status_effects.explanation: Present-day captivity has stripped Albertine of the color and value she had when free, per the narrator's own explicit accounting.
By keeping Albertine captive the narrator no longer suffers jealousy over other women, who become admirable again rather than threatening; his own position eases even as hers diminishes.
The remembered affront still wounds him, reviving shame and jealousy tied to the moment Albertine mocked him before a rival.
The same memory that wounds the narrator paradoxically restores Albertine's beauty and value in his eyes, admired by another and recalled as the loveliest among her friends on the beach.
